questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}+2y=13\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),\,y(0)=5
$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}+2y=13\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x},$ solve the initial value problem.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $13\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}=-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))+2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))=13\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(3\beta +2\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+(-3\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=13\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3\beta +2\alpha =13\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)) \\ -3\alpha +2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =2,\beta =3.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Now, we can find the constant $A$ using the initial conditions.

Substituting $y(0)=5$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{-2\cdot 0}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0) & =5 \\ A+2+0 & =5 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=3{e}^{-2x}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).
$$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}3 & -9 & 6 \\ 4 & -12 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -9 & 6 \\ 4 & -12 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 \\ 4 & -12 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(f∘u)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(u) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(2u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\,({u}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2u \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘u)^{′}(t) & =f′(u(t))u′(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2u(t) \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2(2t+2) \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot 2 \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8t+8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following are affine transformations?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2} \\ v-u\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}6v-4u \\ 3u+3v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v+9 \\ v-9\end{aligned}]$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not affine since it contains the quadratic terms ${u}^{2}$ and ${v}^{2}.$

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is affine. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6v-4u \\ 3u+3v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4u+6v \\ 3u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

In fact, the transformation ${T}_{2}$ is a linear transformation.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is affine. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+v+9 \\ v-9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{2}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only."
